title: Trade Networks: Silk Road and Hanseatic League
welcome_lead: From Samarkand caravans to Baltic kontors, follow the merchants who connected the medieval world.
meta_desc: History Society & Economy 750-1400 Adventure 3: Silk Road, Hanseatic League and medieval trade.
final_note: You have crossed deserts and seas with medieval traders. Networks of trust and credit were as vital as wagons and ships.

walkthroughs.body_html: Silk, spices, paper, gunpowder and porcelain travelled west; silver, wool, glass and Christian and Islamic religious ideas travelled east. Cities like Samarkand, Bukhara, Kashgar and Dunhuang flourished as nodes. Mongol unification under Genghis Khan and his successors briefly created an unusually safe corridor exploited by travellers like Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta.

In the Baltic and North Seas, north German merchants — initially from Lübeck — banded together to defend privileges in foreign ports. By the late 13th century the Hanseatic League linked dozens of towns from Novgorod to Bruges, dealing in furs, fish, grain, timber, amber and salt.

Italian banking innovations — bills of exchange, double-entry bookkeeping, maritime insurance — supported expanding trade. The development of partnerships such as the commenda shared risk and capital, while fairs in Champagne and elsewhere acted as clearing houses linking northern and southern networks.
